nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-01.title: Find the extremes
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-01.body:
The smallest 3-digit accessible integer has digits 1, 2, 4: $124$ (since $1\mid124$, $2\mid124$, $4\mid124$).

For the largest, digits 9, 3, 6 give $936$ ($936/9=104$, $936/3=312$, $936/6=156$). One can verify no arrangement with hundreds digit 9 gives a larger accessible integer.

$936-124=\mathbf{812}$.

**Answer: 812**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-02.title: Factor and simplify
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-02.body: Note $x(x+3)=x^2+3x$ and $(x+1)(x+2)=x^2+3x+2$. Let $u=x^2+3x+1$; then the radicand is $(u-1)(u+1)+1=u^2$, so $\sqrt{\cdots}=|u|=|x^2+3x+1|$. At $x=-2.013$, $x^2+3x+1\approx4.052-6.039+1<0$, so $|u|=-(x^2+3x+1)$. The denominator is $x+\tfrac{1}{x}+3=\tfrac{x^2+3x+1}{x}$. Thus the expression equals $\dfrac{-(x^2+3x+1)}{(x^2+3x+1)/x}=-x=2.013$. **Answer: 2.013**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-03.title: Use the digit sum
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-03.body:
$\overline{ABC}+\overline{BCA}+\overline{CAB}=111(A+B+C)=3\cdot37\cdot(A+B+C)$. Since $p$ divides each number it divides their sum, so $p\mid3\cdot37\cdot(A+B+C)$. Thus $p\in\{3,37\}$ (or $p\mid(A+B+C)$, but $A+B+C\le24$ limits that). Check $p=37$: take $A=1,B=4,C=8$: $148=37\cdot4$, $481=37\cdot13$, $814=37\cdot22$. ✓

**Answer: 37**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-04.title: Medians from right angles
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-04.body:
Since $\angle ADB=90°$ (foot of altitude), $F$ (midpoint of hypotenuse $AB$) satisfies $DF=AF=5$. Similarly $EF=5$. So $\triangle DEF$ is isosceles with $DF=EF=5$. Using $m\angle C=60°$ and angle chasing, $m\angle DFE=60°$, making $\triangle DEF$ equilateral. Area $=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot25=\dfrac{25\sqrt3}{4}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{25\sqrt3}{4}$**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-05.title: Square both sides
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-05.body:
Squaring: $1-\sin\theta=\sin^2\theta-2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta=1-2\sin\theta\cos\theta$. So $\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)=0$: $\sin\theta=0$ (excluded from $(0°,180°)$ since $\theta=180°$ is excluded) or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, giving $\theta=60°$. Check RHS at $60°$: $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}-\tfrac12>0$ ✓, and squaring confirms. Only solution is $60°$.

**Answer: 60°**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-06.title: Factor $x^{11}+x+1$
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-06.body:
$12^{11}+13=12^{11}+12+1$. The polynomial $x^{11}+x+1$ is divisible by $1+x+x^2$ (since the exponents $0,1,11$ partition mod 3 as $\{0,1,2\}$, the cube roots of unity are roots). At $x=12$: $1+12+144=157$ divides $12^{11}+12+1$. Computing $12^{11}+13=157\times4{,}732{,}537{,}393$, and $4{,}732{,}537{,}393$ is prime (verified). The smaller prime is $157$.

**Answer: 157**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-08.title: Angle chase
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-08.body:
Let $m\angle FAD=2x$. Since $\triangle FAD$ is isosceles ($AF=AD$), $m\angle AFD=m\angle ADF=90°-x$, so $m\angle BFD=90°+x$. Since $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles, $m\angle B=m\angle C$. With $m\angle BAC=m\angle FAD+m\angle DAC=2x+54°$, we get $m\angle B=\frac{180°-(2x+54°)}{2}=63°-x$. In $\triangle BFD$: $(63°-x)+(90°+x)+m\angle FDB=180°$, so $m\angle FDB=27°$.

**Answer: 27°**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-09.title: Linear remainder via derivatives
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-09.body:
Write $f(x)=x^{20}+x^{13}+1$. The remainder on division by $(x-1)^2$ is linear, $ax+b$, so $f(x)=(x-1)^2q(x)+ax+b$.

Setting $x=1$: $a+b=f(1)=3$. Differentiating and setting $x=1$: $a=f'(1)=20+13=33$. So $b=3-33=-30$.

**Answer: $33x-30$**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-10.title: Stars and bars
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-10.body:
A 3-digit ascending integer satisfies $1\le a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le9$ (no leading zero since $a_1\ge1$). Let $b_1=a_1-1,\,b_2=a_2-a_1,\,b_3=a_3-a_2,\,b_4=9-a_3\ge0$; then $b_1+b_2+b_3+b_4=8$. By stars and bars: $\binom{11}{3}=165$.

**Answer: 165**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-11.title: Contradiction for $n=4$
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-11.body:
If $n\ge4$: $(a_1+a_2+a_3)+(a_2+a_3+a_4)>0$ (sum of two positive triples). But this equals $(a_1+a_2)+(a_2+a_3)+(a_3+a_4)$, the sum of three consecutive pairs, each negative — contradiction. So $n\le3$. The sequence $2,-3,2$ satisfies all conditions ($2+(-3)+2=1>0$; $2+(-3)=-1<0$; $(-3)+2=-1<0$). So $n=3$ is achievable.

**Answer: 3**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-12.title: Area ratios via cevians
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-12.body:
Let $x=[DEF]$ and $y=[BCF]$, where $[\,]$ denotes area.

Triangles $BDF$ and $DEF$ share the height from $D$ to line $BE$, and triangles $BCF$ and $CEF$ share the height from $C$, so $\dfrac{BF}{FE}=\dfrac{1}{x}=\dfrac{y}{3}$, i.e. $y=\dfrac{3}{x}$.

Similarly, $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{[ADE]}{[DBE]}=\dfrac{[ADC]}{[DBC]}$, so $\dfrac{4}{x+1}=\dfrac{x+7}{y+1}$, i.e. $x^2+8x+7=4y+4$.

Substituting $y=3/x$ gives $x^3+8x^2+3x-12=0$, whose only positive root is $x=1$. Then $y=3$, and $[ABC]=1+3+4+x+y=12$.

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-13.title: Count by digit position
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-13.body:
**Units digits.** Among $1$–$30$, each odd digit $1,3,5,7,9$ appears as a units digit three times (in $1$–$9$, $11$–$19$ and $21$–$29$), contributing $3(1+3+5+7+9)=75$.

**Tens digits.** The tens digit $1$ appears in $10$–$19$ (ten times), contributing $10$; the tens digit $3$ appears once (in $30$), contributing $3$.

Total: $75+10+3=88$.

**Answer: 88**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-14.title: Angle chasing
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-14.body:
The vertices lie on a circle and each side cuts off an arc of $40^\circ$.

Chords $A_1A_3$ and $A_2A_6$ meet at $B$, so $m\angle A_1BA_2=\tfrac12(\widehat{A_1A_2}+\widehat{A_3A_6})=\tfrac12(40^\circ+120^\circ)=80^\circ$. Also $m\angle A_1A_2A_6=\tfrac12\widehat{A_6A_1}=\tfrac12(160^\circ)=80^\circ$. Hence $\triangle A_1A_2B$ is isosceles with $A_1B=A_1A_2=A_1A_9$.

So $\triangle A_9A_1B$ is isosceles. Its apex angle is $m\angle A_9A_1A_3=\tfrac12\widehat{A_3A_9}=\tfrac12(240^\circ)=120^\circ$, so $m\angle A_9BA_1=\tfrac12(180^\circ-120^\circ)=30^\circ$.

**Answer: 30°**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-15.title: Acute conditions
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-15.body:
By the triangle inequality, $5<m<15$, so $m\in\{6,\dots,14\}$.

If $m\le10$, the longest side is $10$, and the triangle is acute iff $5^2+m^2>10^2$, i.e. $m^2>75$, so $m\in\{9,10\}$.

If $m>10$, the longest side is $m$, and the triangle is acute iff $m^2<5^2+10^2=125$, so $m=11$.

The acute values are $m=9,10,11$.

**Answer: 3**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-16.title: Case analysis
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-16.body:
Since $\lceil x-1\rceil$ and $\lfloor x+1\rfloor$ are integers, their product is prime only if one factor is $\pm1$ and the other is $\pm p$ with the same sign.

- $1<x\le2$: $\lceil x-1\rceil=1$ and $\lfloor x+1\rfloor\in\{2,3\}$, so the product is $2$ or $3$, prime.
- $-2\le x<-1$: $\lfloor x+1\rfloor=-1$ and $\lceil x-1\rceil\in\{-3,-2\}$, so the product is $3$ or $2$, prime.
- $-1\le x\le1$: one factor is $0$.
- $x>2$: both factors are at least $2$, so the product is composite; similarly for $x<-2$ both factors are at most $-2$.

**Answer: $1<x\le2$ or $-2\le x<-1$**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-17.title: Product formula for sines
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-17.body:
Use the identity $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\sin\dfrac{k\pi}{n}=\dfrac{n}{2^{n-1}}$. With $n=180$, the angle $\dfrac{k\pi}{180}$ is $k^\circ$, so
$$(\sin1^\circ)(\sin2^\circ)\cdots(\sin179^\circ)=\frac{180}{2^{179}}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{180}{2^{179}}$**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-18.title: Equal roots by AM-GM
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-18.body:
If all 9 roots are real with sum $3$ (from Vieta's: sum = 3) and $\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=4$ (coefficient of $x^7$ is 4, so $e_2=4$), then $\sum r_i^2=(\sum r_i)^2-2\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=9-8=1$. The variance $\sum(r_i-\bar r)^2=\sum r_i^2-9\bar r^2=1-9(1/3)^2=1-1=0$. So all roots equal $\frac{1}{3}$, and $P(x)=\left(x-\frac13\right)^9$. The coefficient of $x^6$ is $\binom{9}{3}\left(-\frac13\right)^3=84\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{27}\right)=-\frac{28}{9}$.

**Answer: $-\dfrac{28}{9}$**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-19.title: Parity argument
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-19.body:
If $b$ is odd, $7b+3$ is even and greater than 2 (for reasonable $b$), so composite. Thus $b$ must be even. If $b$ is even, $44-3b$ is even. For it to be prime, $44-3b=2$, giving $b=14$. Check: $2013-14=1999$ (prime ✓), $44-42=2$ (prime ✓), $98+3=101$ (prime ✓).

**Answer: 14**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-20.title: Complement counting
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-20.body:
The leading digit of an $n$-digit number is one of $1$–$9$, and each of the other $n-1$ digits is one of $0$–$9$. So the probability of containing no $0$ is $\left(\tfrac{9}{10}\right)^{n-1}$, and we need $\left(\tfrac{9}{10}\right)^{n-1}<\tfrac12$.

Since $0.9^6\approx0.531>0.5$ and $0.9^7\approx0.478<0.5$, we need $n-1\ge7$, so $n=8$.

**Answer: 8**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-21.title: Powers of 3
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-21.body: $\log_9 x$ is rational iff $x=3^{2k/m}$ for integers $k,m$, i.e., $x$ is an integer power of 3. Among $1,\ldots,2013$: the powers of 3 are $3^0,3^1,3^2,3^3,3^4,3^5,3^6$ (since $3^7=2187>2013$). Then $f(3^j)=\log_9(3^j)=j/2$. Sum $=0+\tfrac{1}{2}+1+\tfrac{3}{2}+2+\tfrac{5}{2}+3=\tfrac{21}{2}$.

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-22.title: Inscribed angles
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-22.body: Since $AD$ is a diameter, $\angle ACD=90°$ (angle in semicircle). The radius $OB=OC=5$ and $BC=5$, so $\triangle BOC$ is equilateral and arc $BC=60°$. The external angle at $E$ satisfies $m\angle AED=\tfrac{1}{2}(\text{arc }AD-\text{arc }BC)=\tfrac{1}{2}(180°-60°)=60°$.

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-23.title: Inclusion-exclusion
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-23.body: There are 90 choices for $AB$ (10–99). For each, $AB=CD$ with any units digit $E$: $90\times10=900$ five-digit integers. For $AB=DE$ with any middle digit $C$: $90\times10=900$. By inclusion-exclusion, subtract $AB=CD=DE$: this forces $C=A$, $D=B$, $D=A$, $E=B$, so $A=B$; that gives 9 choices. Total: $900+900-9=1791$.

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-24.title: Find the roots
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-24.body: Setting $x=11$: $0\cdot P(33)=27\cdot13\cdot P(6)$, so $P(6)=0$. Setting $x=-2$: $(-13)P(-6)=0$, so $P(-6)=0$. The functional equation forces degree 3; write $P(x)=a(x-6)(x+3)(x+6)$. From $P(1)=a(-5)(4)(7)=-140a=-280$, so $a=2$. Then $P(2)=2(-4)(5)(8)=-320$.

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-25.title: Factor 2013 and find threshold
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-25.body:
$2013=3\cdot11\cdot61$, so $2013^2=3^2\cdot11^2\cdot61^2$. For $61^2\mid(n!)!$, we need at least two multiples of 61 among $\{1,\ldots,n!\}$, i.e., $n!\ge122$. Since $5!=120<122$ and $6!=720\ge122$, the minimum is $n=6$. The constraints from $3^2$ and $11^2$ require $n!$ to be much smaller and are satisfied earlier.

**Answer: 6**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-26.title: Divisor analysis
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-26.body: Four-expressible even number $4k$ satisfies $k=mn$ with positive integers $m<n$. The number of representations is $(\tau(k)-1)/2$ when $k$ is non-square. For exactly 4 representations, $\tau(k)=9$ (giving a perfect square, excluded) or $\tau(k)=8$. The smallest $k>503$ (so $4k>2012$) with $\tau(k)=8$ is $k=506=2\cdot11\cdot23$, giving $4k=2024$.

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-27.title: Divisibility by 11
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-27.body:
Let the number be $\overline{ABC}$. Divisibility by $11$ means $11\mid A-B+C$, and we also need $11\mid A+B+C$. Then $11$ divides the difference $2B$, so $B=0$ and $11\mid A+C$.

Since $1\le A+C\le18$, $A+C=11$ with digits $A\in\{2,\dots,9\}$, $C=11-A$. That gives $209,308,407,506,605,704,803,902$.

**Answer: 8**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-28.title: Count intersecting pairs
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-28.body:
A regular $n$-gon has $\binom{n}{2}-n$ diagonals. For $n=9$: $\binom{9}{2}-9=27$ diagonals. Number of diagonal pairs: $\binom{27}{2}=351$. Two diagonals of a convex polygon intersect inside iff their four endpoints are all distinct and form a convex quadrilateral — equivalently, any 4 vertices determine exactly one interior intersection. Intersecting pairs $=\binom{9}{4}=126$. Probability $=\dfrac{126}{351}=\dfrac{14}{39}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{14}{39}$**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-29.title: Simplify the expression
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-29.body:
Since $\dfrac{(s+3)!}{(s+1)!}=(s+3)(s+2)$ and $\dfrac{s!}{(s+1)!}=\dfrac1{s+1}$, the expression is $\dfrac{(s+3)(s+2)}{s+1}$.

Because $\gcd(s+1,s+2)=1$ and $\gcd(s+1,s+3)\mid2$, the reduced denominator is even exactly when $s+1$ is even and contains a higher power of $2$ than $s+3$. Of the consecutive even numbers $s+1$ and $s+3$, one is $\equiv2\pmod4$, so we need $4\mid s+1$, i.e. $s\equiv3\pmod4$.

There are $25$ such $s$ in $\{1,\dots,100\}$, so the probability is $\dfrac{25}{100}=\dfrac14$.

**Answer: $\dfrac14$**

nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-30.title: Palindrome constraints
nyciml-2013-14-fall-seniora-30.body:
Four-digit palindromes $\overline{ABBA}$ with the same $A$ differ by multiples of $110$, and the only gap smaller than $100$ is $11$, between $\overline{A99A}$ and the next palindrome $\overline{(A+1)00(A+1)}$. Since the erased number has two digits, it is $11$ and $a=\overline{A99A}$.

The sum of all two-digit numbers is $4905$, so $a<4905$ and $a\in\{1991,2992,3993\}$, giving $bc=\frac{a}{11}\in\{181,272,363\}$.

- $181$ is prime, so it is not a product of two two-digit numbers.
- $363=11\cdot33$ is the only such factorization, but $11$ was erased.
- $272=16\cdot17$ works.

So $b+c=16+17=33$.

**Answer: 33**
